summary: This specification describes version 2 of the Optimized Link State Routing Protocol (OLSRv2) for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs). It lets wireless devices without fixed infrastructure share routes with one another.

plainLanguage.summary: OLSRv2 lets routers in a changing mobile network keep routes ready before data needs them. Each router selects nearby helpers to reduce how many devices repeat control messages and advertise network links.

subtitle: A proactive routing protocol that reduces control traffic in changing mobile ad hoc networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile ad hoc networks have changing links and no central routing point. Flooding every link-state message from every router creates unnecessary traffic.
tldr.mechanism: Routers select flooding and routing multipoint relays to reduce message forwarding and the topology information they advertise, then calculate routes from that information.
tldr.outcome: OLSRv2 keeps routes available without route discovery delays and has been updated by RFC 7183, RFC 7187, RFC 7188 and RFC 7466.

today: RFC 7181 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7183, RFC 7187, RFC 7188 and RFC 7466. The RFC states that it does not obsolete RFC 3626, which remains for further experimentation.

sections.title: What OLSRv2 Is For
sections.content:
The Optimized Link State Routing Protocol version 2 (OLSRv2) is a proactive routing protocol for Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs). Routers exchange topology information regularly, so routes are maintained before data is sent. This avoids delays for route discovery.

OLSRv2 is designed for changing network layouts and links that may lose messages. It works without a central entity and makes no assumptions about the underlying link layer. It uses the Neighborhood Discovery Protocol and the general MANET packet and message format.
sections.plainLanguage: OLSRv2 keeps routes ready in a mobile network whose connections can change. Routers exchange information without relying on a central controller.

sections.title: How Multipoint Relays Reduce Traffic
sections.content:
Each router selects two sets of multipoint relays (MPRs) from its symmetric, or two-way, one-hop neighbors. Each set covers the router's symmetric two-hop neighbors. Flooding MPRs reduce how many routers retransmit control messages. Routing MPRs reduce how many routers need to advertise link state.

A router retransmits a flooded message only when it first receives it from a router that selected it as a flooding MPR. HELLO messages share local neighbor information and are not forwarded. Topology Control (TC) messages carry selected network information and are flooded using the MPR rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A router chooses nearby relays that together reach its neighbors two steps away. Only selected relays repeat network-wide messages, which reduces control traffic.

sections.title: Selecting Flooding and Routing MPRs
sections.content:
Routers MUST select flooding and routing MPR sets from willing symmetric one-hop neighbors. A valid set covers two-hop neighbors that cannot be reached directly and preserves the minimum-distance route to each two-hop neighbor. An implementation may use any selection process that satisfies the specified properties, so routers can interoperate even if their algorithms differ.

Willingness values express whether a neighbor is available to relay messages or act as an intermediate router. A value of WILL_NEVER excludes the neighbor from that role, while WILL_ALWAYS requires its selection. The two MPR sets are calculated separately because they serve different purposes and may use different link metrics.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router selects willing neighbors that cover the required two-hop neighbors. It can choose different helpers for relaying messages and for building routes.

sections.title: Link Metrics and Timing
sections.content:
OLSRv2 supports directional link metrics. A route's metric is the sum of its link metrics, and the protocol selects routes with the lowest total. The RFC does not define the physical meaning of a metric or how a router determines incoming metric values.

Routers may use different parameter values. Proposed values include a TC message interval of 5 seconds and a TC hop limit of 255. TC messages are sent regularly, with jitter allowed; they MUST NOT be sent only in response to local changes because a router cannot know when distant routers join.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can score links and choose a route with the lowest total score. The specification suggests timing values, but routers may use different settings.

sections.title: HELLO and TC Messages
sections.content:
OLSRv2 extends HELLO messages with information such as a router's identity, link metrics, willingness, and MPR selections. HELLO messages describe nearby links and are not forwarded. TC messages advertise selected topology information throughout the MANET.

TC messages carry an originator address, sequence information, a hop limit, validity information, and advertised neighbors or attached networks. A sequence number lets a router distinguish newer topology information from older information that arrived later. Complete TC messages describe all advertised selectors; incomplete messages can report additions.
sections.plainLanguage: HELLO messages describe a router's nearby links and relay choices. TC messages share selected network information, with sequence numbers to distinguish newer updates from older ones.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
False or replayed routing messages can corrupt the network's view of its links. The RFC says message authentication is strongly advised and explains that timestamps or sequence numbers help identify replayed information. Confidentiality may also matter because control messages can reveal network topology.

A conformant implementation MUST implement the integrity and replay protection specified in RFC 7183. That mechanism uses a timestamp and an Integrity Check Value based on HMAC with SHA-256 and manually managed shared keys. Longer deployments should consider other mechanisms, such as rekeying.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need to check that control messages are genuine and recent. OLSRv2 implementations must support the integrity and replay protection specified in RFC 7183.
